ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
There exists a uniform electric field in space, directed diagonally upward at an angle of \(45^{\circ}\) to the horizontal, with an electric field strength of \(E=\frac{\sqrt{2}m g}{q}\), and the field is sufficiently extensive. Within this electric field, there is an insulating barrier MN, inclined at an angle of \(\theta=45^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. A small positively charged ball with mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) is projected vertically upward from point \(O\), which is at the same horizontal level as point \(M\), with an initial velocity \(v_{0}\). The ball moves in such a way that it just avoids colliding with the barrier, and the plane of the ball's trajectory is perpendicular to the barrier. The acceleration due to gravity is \(g\).

1. What is the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball when it is close to the baffle?
2. What is the distance from point $M$ when the small ball is close to the baffle?

Within this electric field, there is an insulating barrier MN, inclined at an angle of \(\theta=45^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. A small positively charged ball with mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) is projected vertically upward from point \(O\), which is at the same horizontal level as point \(M\), with an initial velocity \(v_{0}\). ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the inclined baffle MN extends from point M at the lower left to point N at the upper right, and the baffle makes an angle θ with the horizontal dashed line; point O is to the right of point M and is on the same horizontal line as M; the small ball is launched at point O with a vertically upward initial velocity v0, and the dashed trajectory in the figure bends toward the upper right and is tangent to the baffle near the baffle, indicating "just not touching the baffle". Then reason: According to the specified method, take M as the origin, horizontally rightward as the x-axis, and vertically upward as the y-axis. The electric field strength E=√2mg/q, and the direction makes 45° with the horizontal, so the horizontal and vertical components of the electric force qE are both mg. In the vertical direction, the electric force mg is upward and gravity mg is downward, and the two cancel; in the horizontal direction, only the electric force remains to provide acceleration, so a_x=g, a_y=0. Let the coordinates of point O be (d,0). The initial velocity of the small ball is vertically upward, so the equations of motion are x=d+gt^2/2, y=v0 t. The baffle MN makes 45° with the horizontal and passes through point M, so the straight line where the baffle lies is y=x. The small ball just avoids the baffle, indicating that the trajectory is tangent to the straight line y=x near the baffle. The trajectory slope dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt)=v0/(gt). At tangency, the slope equals the baffle slope 1, so v0/(gt)=1, giving t=v0/g. Substitute into the equations of motion: y=v0·(v0/g)=v0^2/g; x=d+g(v0/g)^2/2=d+v0^2/(2g). The tangency point is on the baffle y=x, so x=y=v0^2/g, therefore d=v0^2/(2g). The coordinates of the tangency point are (v0^2/g, v0^2/g). At this time the velocity components are v_x=gt=v0, v_y=v0, so the speed magnitude v=√(v0^2+v0^2)=√2 v0. The distance from the tangency point to point M along the baffle is √(x^2+y^2)=√[(v0^2/g)^2+(v0^2/g)^2]=√2 v0^2/g.
